In contrast, let's look at a much better biopic, the brilliant Joe Wright film Darkest Hour about Winston Churchill. Wright made a decision with this film that was so inspired, I began to wonder if it was the only acceptable way to present a biopic. He used the character of Elizabeth Layton, Churchill's secretary, a slightly fictionalized version of Churchill's actual secretary, to serve as a kind of every man or every woman on whose shoulders we could perch as she was drawn quite by chance into the orbit of Churchill's life. The story is told often from her perspective, which is brilliant for a number of reasons. First, it removes the pressure from the main subject, that is Churchill, who no longer needs to carry the film so much as occupy it. The space filled by him is the space seen by Miss Layton. Additionally, framing Churchill's life in the view of this outsider allowed Wright to remove himself just enough from the inside of Churchill's mind. Instead, he took a step back and allowed the viewer to observe him from the outside as Miss Layton had done, thereby making their own interpretations and judgments. Villains, or if you like antagonists, are an essential component of any story. This can take a whole assortment of forms.

Basically, antagonist really only means that the hero, or protagonist, has to have some significant resistance to his ultimate narrative goal.

For that reason, you can get aaway with things like the environment being the antagonist in disaster movies, or the protagonist himself being his own worst enemy in certain kinds of dramatic stories.

Or both. A villain is really just the opposition to the hero's goal. That being said, villains, that is to say bad guys, have been experiencing a strange evolution in the last few decades, especially more recently.

For one thing, they have become less and less villainous. Taking it further, they have become less and less evil.

Part of this is in an effort in modern and postmodern literature to provide all aspects of a story with more multidimensional realism.

Naturally, a villain would be a human or human adjacent, so there ought to be more to him than just being the bad guy.

Maybe we ought to examine how he came to be the bad guy, or whether or not his goals might have some merit.

All of this ostensibly in the pursuit of richer characters, which is not an unworthy pursuit, but let's tackle this issue one piece at a time.

All of this literary experimentation has its place, I suppose, if you do it right, which, as I said, we'll get into in a bit here.

But something that we as a society have apparently forgotten is that most of the time, a crucial factor in the villain's character is evil.

Of course, I don't mean that all characters need to be Lucifer as Morningstar or even Morgoth, although huge, ugly, powerful evil is actually a crucial aspect of fiction that is currently all but extinct.

What I mean is that the clear moral judgment and acceptance that the villain character is morally bad in some major significant way is a critical part of making a villain.

That is, they won't just remain at a higher level, but their reading ability grows faster depending on how high it was to start with.

But if a child starts lower, then he or she will remain lower in terms of level and skill.

Many believe that no matter where a child starts at all eventually evens out, more or less.

The Matthew Effect means that this is not true. This study, insofar as any study can, proved the validity of the Matthew Effect.

This goes back a little to what I was saying in my reading education video, that there are some people who believe that children have an innate skill for reading and it just has to be unlocked.

Obviously, that's nonsense. So how that ties into the Matthew Effect is that a child isn't locked into whatever skill they happen to have the second they start to be able to sound out words.

They develop skills with practice. In a sense, it's parents and to a lesser extent teachers who have control over this.

Parents are encouraged to find challenging but still age-appropriate books for their kids to read.

And children are encouraged to to bring those books to mom or dad or teacher and say, what does this word mean?

And so they reach an age when they learn how to look up the meanings themselves, preferably in a physical paper dictionary and not a smartphone.

The point I'm trying to make is that kids, and you know, people, are not predestined with some locked-in reading level.

The more you challenge yourself and the earlier you start, the more and faster your vocabulary will grow.

Forming a habit as a young child to read texts that are a hair above your level informs your entire development going forward.

But it can be really frustrating to finish a mini-arc and have to figure out that ever elusive, what happens next. Which leads me to the final, crucially important part of the storytelling principle. Each of these mini-arcs must lead to the next. You can't just have one mini-arc and then the action crests and then you have another random mini-arc. The events of arc 1 must lead to arc 2. Put a different way, you can easily figure out the events of arc 2 by asking yourself what would be the result of the events of arc 1. So using our previous example, after Johnny Safecracker was interrupted from finishing one robbery when he was abducted by a mob boss, what could happen because of that? Well maybe the guy who hired him to do the first robbery will be a little angry that that job didn't get done. And now you know what your next mini-arc could be. Do you see what I mean? The path is already there, you just have to find it. And there is no one path. The thing that happens next could be one of a hundred equally great choices. That part's up to you, the writer.
